questions.q: You are extracting fields from hundreds of invoices. What goes in the system prompt and what goes in the user message?
options: Everything goes in the user message so the model sees it all at once
The invoice text goes in the system prompt and the rules go in the user message
Role, rules and what to do when a field is missing go in the system prompt; each invoice's text goes in the user message inside tags
Only the model id goes in the system prompt
questions.why: Stable instructions belong in the system prompt and changing data belongs in the user message.

questions.q: Using structured outputs, the model returns JSON that matches your schema, but the total is 0 and the supplier name is not in the invoice. What does this tell you?
options: A schema guarantees shape, not truth, so you also need business rules such as checking values appear in the source text
The schema is broken and must be rewritten
Structured outputs failed and you should go back to plain text
This cannot happen when structured outputs are used
questions.why: Parsing into a typed object is step one; business rules catch values that are well formed but wrong.

questions.q: A response comes back with finish_reason 'length'. What should your code do?
options: Use it as normal, since the model finished
Treat it as a refusal and stop the whole run
Ignore finish_reason, the JSON parser will catch any problem
Treat the output as possibly cut off and handle it on purpose
questions.why: length means the model ran out of room, so the output may be incomplete. Handle it on purpose instead of assuming success.

questions.q: Your batch run over a folder of 200 invoices stops completely when one corrupt file throws an error. What is the fix?
options: Remove corrupt files by hand before every run
Catch exceptions per item, write an error record for that item and carry on
Switch to a larger model that can read corrupt files
Run the folder one file at a time by hand
questions.why: Each item should return a validated object or an error record so one bad file does not stop the run.

questions.q: A reply has a tool call asking for get_order_status with order_id 'A-1002'. What does your code do next?
options: Add the reply to the history, run the function, send a tool message with the matching tool_call_id, then call the model again
Read the final answer from the reply, since the model already ran the tool
Send the order id back as plain text in a new user message
Drop the reply and send only the function output
questions.why: The model only proposes the call; your code runs it and returns a matched tool message before the next request.

questions.q: The order lookup finds no order with the id the model sent. What should go back to the model?
options: Nothing, skip the tool message for that call
An empty string so the model guesses the status
A tool message that says clearly the call failed, such as 'no order with that id'
A full stack trace so the model can debug it
questions.why: A clear error result lets the model ask the user for a correct id instead of inventing an answer.

questions.q: The model calls get_order_status with an order id that belongs to a different customer. Why should your function still check before running it?
options: It should not check, the schema already validated the input
It only needs to check if the order id is longer than usual
The model has already confirmed the user owns the order
The model choosing a tool is not the same as the user being allowed to use it, so validate format and permissions in code
questions.why: Your code decides what is allowed; the schema checks shape, not the user's rights.

questions.q: The model keeps calling the wrong tool. One tool's description is just 'Gets order'. What is the best first fix?
options: Merge all tools into one large tool with many modes
Rewrite the description to say what the tool does, when to use it and what the inputs mean, with an example
Remove the system prompt so the model focuses on tools
Force that tool on every turn with tool_choice
questions.why: The model picks and fills tools mostly from the description, so a specific description is the main lever.

questions.q: Your SOP assistant gives wrong answers for several questions. What do you check first?
options: What was retrieved for those questions
Swap to a larger model
Rewrite the system prompt
Add more chunks to every prompt
questions.why: Most RAG problems are retrieval problems: the right chunk was missed, split or ranked too low.

questions.q: Users ask questions full of exact product codes and policy names. For a first POC, which search approach fits best?
options: Embedding search only, since keywords never work for questions
No search, just put every document in the prompt
Keyword search, such as SQLite FTS5, which is strong on exact terms and easy to debug
A new embedding model trained on their documents
questions.why: Keyword search is simple, fast and excellent for exact terms like product codes, and often enough to prove value.

questions.q: An employee asks about train travel, but the retrieved policy chunks only cover flights. What should a well-built RAG answer do?
options: Give a sensible general rule about train travel
Answer using the flight rules, since travel is travel
Return the full travel policy for the user to read
Say the provided policy does not cover it, because the prompt tells the model to say it does not know when sources lack the answer
questions.why: The 'I do not know' instruction is what stops the model filling gaps with plausible guesses.

questions.q: A retailer says 'we want an agent' for damaged order emails. The steps are: look up the order, check fixed rules, draft a reply and a refund for approval. What do you recommend?
options: An autonomous agent with refund rights, since the client asked for an agent
Build a fixed workflow first, and add an agent only for the messy cases it cannot handle
A multi-agent system with one agent per step
No AI at all, because refunds are risky
questions.why: If you can draw the steps in advance, a workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test.

questions.q: Which task is the best fit for an agent rather than a workflow?
options: Investigating why a shipment is late across several systems, where the next step depends on what is found
Classifying each email into one of five fixed categories
Extracting the same four fields from every invoice
Sending a weekly report built from a fixed query
questions.why: Agents fit when the number and order of steps cannot be known in advance.

questions.q: Your agent has a turn limit, read-only tools by default and approval for refunds. Where should these guardrails be enforced?
options: Only in the system prompt, as clear instructions
In the tool descriptions, so the model reads them
In code around the loop, so they hold even when the model makes a poor choice
In a weekly review of the logs
questions.why: Turn limits, tool permissions and approvals belong in code, not only in the prompt.

questions.q: You are building one custom app with two tools that no other app will ever use. Is an MCP server worth it?
options: Yes, every tool must be an MCP server
Yes, because MCP makes the model more accurate
No, because MCP only works with remote servers
Probably not; plain tool use inside the app is simpler, and you can move the functions to MCP later
questions.why: MCP pays off when a capability is shared across hosts or a ready-made server exists; otherwise it adds moving parts.

questions.q: After adding print statements for debugging, your local stdio MCP server stops working in the host. Why?
options: A stdio server talks through standard output, so prints break the protocol messages; log to standard error instead
Print statements slow the server past the host's timeout
The host blocks any server that writes logs
Prints change the tool's input schema
questions.why: Standard output carries the protocol messages in the stdio transport.

questions.q: An MCP server offers tools, resources and prompts. Who decides when a tool is called?
options: The user, by picking it from a list
The model
The application, by attaching it to context
The MCP server, on a schedule
questions.why: The model calls tools, the application or user picks resources, and the user picks prompts.

questions.q: You ask a coding assistant to make a failing test pass, and it edits the test to expect the wrong value. How do you prevent this?
options: Let it, since a passing test means the work is done
Turn off tests so the assistant cannot touch them
Say in the brief that tests are fixed and must not be changed without asking, and read the diff yourself
Ask it to write more tests next time
questions.why: Assistants may weaken or delete tests to get a pass, so the brief fixes them and your review catches changes.

questions.q: What single habit most improves results from an AI coding assistant, according to the lesson?
options: Writing very long project memory files
Doing everything in one long session so it remembers more
Letting it run any command without approval
Giving it a check it can run itself, such as a test suite, so it loops until the check passes
questions.why: With a runnable check the assistant does not stop when the code merely looks done.

questions.q: Deep into a long session, you have corrected the assistant on the same mistake twice. What should you do?
options: Start a fresh session with a better brief that includes what you learned
Keep correcting it in the same session until it learns
Paste the whole codebase into the chat for more context
Switch to a different editor plugin
questions.why: As the context window fills, quality drops, and a fresh start with a sharper brief works better.
